citation: Main: Kerry Muhlestein, 'Execration Ritual', in Jacco Dieleman and Willeke Wendrich (eds.), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (UEE) 1(1), Los Angeles, Version 1, April 2008 (eScholarship publication date 2008-04-03). https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3f6268zf (PDF: https://escholarship.org/content/qt3f6268zf/qt3f6268zf.pdf). Short citation given by UEE: 'Muhlestein, 2008, Execration Ritual. UEE.' Companion: Kerry Muhlestein, 'Violence', in Elizabeth Frood and Willeke Wendrich (eds.), UEE 1(1), Version 1, November 2015 (eScholarship date 2015-11-12). https://escholarship.org/uc/item/9661n6rn.
evidence_tier: Scholarly reference work. Both entries are marked 'Peer reviewed' on eScholarship; UEE is an edited encyclopedia (Area Editor Religion for the 2008 entry, Individual and Society for the 2015 entry). Secondary synthesis, not a primary publication of the finds.
access_status: Both entries fully read as PDFs. eScholarship returned a CloudFront 403 to direct download, so the PDFs were retrieved from Wayback Machine copies of the eScholarship PDF URLs (Execration Ritual: 6 pages including cover; Violence: 6-page PDF file, text extracted with pdftotext). Full text of the Execration Ritual entry (pp. 1-3 plus bibliography) read end to end; Violence entry read in the sections relevant here (abstract, Preternatural Violence, Ritual and cultic violence, symbolic violence/iconography, king and isfet, conclusion on change over time). The underlying primary works (Vila 1963/1973, Ritner 1993, Schott 1929, Faulkner 1936-38) were not opened for this item.
exact_quotes: Execration Ritual, abstract (p. 1): 'The execration ritual was intended to prevent rebellious actions by Egyptians, foreigners, or supernatural forces by textually and kinetically destroying enemies via inanimate, animal, or human substitutes. Execration rites are attested throughout Pharaonic history.'

Execration Ritual, p. 1: 'Execration rituals were stylized magical actions aimed at thwarting or eradicating foes and were similar in nature to other protective measures, such as apotropaic animal sacrifice or walking on depictions of enemies. Execration rites took place from at least early in the Old Kingdom through the Roman Period.'
Execration Ritual, p. 1: 'Over 1,000 execration deposits have been found, mostly in cemeteries, notably at Semna, Uronarti, Mirgissa, Elephantine, Thebes, Balat, Abydos, Helwan, Saqqara, and Giza.'

Execration Ritual, p. 1: 'Important texts include Papyrus Bremner-Rhind, P. Louvre 3129, P. British Museum 10252 , and P. Salt 825. Execration texts could be as simple as lists of forces and people against whom the rite was enacted, or could contain substantial formulae.'

Execration Ritual, p. 1 (origins): 'Assmann (1994: 51) suggests that after red pots were used for offerings they had to be destroyed and that the smashing of these pots was assigned an overlapping meaning of scaring away—or eventually destroying—enemies (cf. Pyramid Texts 23 and 244).'

Execration Ritual, pp. 1-2: 'The text repeatedly notes that those who know creation can also eliminate their own enemies (Faulkner 1937: 172; 1938: 41-42), thus tying the re-creative aspect of purification to execration.'

Execration Ritual, p. 2: 'By the Middle Kingdom execration texts had become standardized (though they would change over time), perhaps indicating that the rite had also taken a standard form. Some execration rites arose due to specific circumstances, but at least by the Late Period there were also both daily and cyclical festival execrations (Faulkner 1937: 169, 171, 174).'

Execration Ritual, p. 2: 'Execration rites could be aimed at political, preternatural, or personal enemies. The political and preternatural were often tied together. The Book of Felling Apophis, for example, instructs that the rite will fell the enemies of Ra, Horus, and Pharaoh (Faulkner 1937: 171, 173-175).'

Execration Ritual, p. 2: 'The victims of these rites were those who, whether dead or alive, would in the future (using the future relative sDmtj.fj form) rebel, conspire rebellion, or think of speaking, sleeping, or dreaming rebelliously, or with ill-intent.'
Execration Ritual, p. 2: 'Versions of execration were carried out both on a large-scale basis by the state and on a small scale by individuals throughout Egyptian history.'

Execration Ritual, p. 2: 'If the Bremner-Rhind Papyrus is any indication, wax figures and a fresh sheet of papyrus, on which the targeted name was written, were among the most commonly used materials. The animals, hair, papyrus, wood, and wax ritual victims are largely archaeologically invisible, making the known (mostly clay) remains of the ritual a vast under-representation of the frequency of the rite.'

Execration Ritual, p. 2 (Mirgissa): 'At the most complete execration find—the Middle Kingdom fortress at Mirgissa—besides the remnants of melted wax, other trace remains indicate the use of nearly 200 broken inscribed red vases, over 400 broken uninscribed red vases, nearly 350 mud figurines, four limestone figures, and one human, whose head was ritually severed and buried upside down as part of the rite (Ritner 1993: 153-154; Vila 1973).'
Execration Ritual, p. 2: 'Similar evidence of human victims as execration figures also appears in an early 18th-Dynasty context at Avaris (Fuscaldo 2003).'

Execration Ritual, p. 2 (actions): 'ritual objects could be bound, smashed (red pots, probably with a pestle), stomped on, stabbed, cut, speared, spat on, locked in a box, burned, and saturated in urine, before (almost always) being buried (sometimes upside down).'

Execration Ritual, pp. 2-3, quoting a rite (Schott 1929: 5): '“spit on him four times . . . trample on him with the left foot . . . smite him with a spear . . . slaughter him with a knife . . . place him on the fire . . . spit on him in the fire many times”'

Execration Ritual, p. 3 (closing): 'A full rite could employ any of these actions numerous times with numerous figures. Thus various magical measures were taken to prevent chaotic forces from acting before they could even begin.'

Execration Ritual, Bibliographic Notes (p. 3): 'The Theban version is found in P. Bremner-Rhind [= P. British Museum 10188] (Faulkner 1936, 1937, 1938).' and 'Gee (fc.) has traced the history of a specific priesthood line that performed the rites for several generations during the Ptolemaic Period and has identified the space within the temple of Montu at Karnak where they performed the ritual.'

Violence (2015), Preternatural Violence (p. 2): 'While such violent enemies represent chaos, their violent destruction represents a restoration of order. This battle often becomes personified, such as the ongoing battle between Apophis and the Sun God, or as in accounts of Seth stabbing and spearing the Chaos serpent.'

Violence (2015), Ritual and cultic violence (p. 5): 'Sometimes the objects were anthropomorphic in form, as with the many clay, stone, and wax figures used in execration rituals (Muhlestein 2008a). During the ceremonies, these figures were smashed, decapitated, mutilated, stabbed, speared, burned, and buried. Violence against mortals and against preternatural enemies was often combined in the rites.'

Violence (2015), pp. 5-6: 'At least two execration rituals, one at Mirgissa during the Middle Kingdom and one at Avaris during the early 18th Dynasty, almost certainly used humans as the objects of the ritual (Muhlestein 2008a, 2008b: 194-196).'

Violence (2015), symbolic violence: 'Violence done to real foreigners and to inanimate representations was aimed at defeating forces of chaos. These were two prongs in the same weapon wielded by the servants of order against chaos.' and 'Thus an ongoing kinetic violence was often a component of violent iconography (for these, see Ritner 1993: 119-179).'
Violence (2015), abstract: 'Improper violence disturbed order while sanctioned violence restored it.'

Violence (2015), p. 10: 'In general, the ideal was that violence was to be avoided. Yet when isfet needed to be destroyed, violence was the appropriate response.' and 'Ritual slaying appears to have remained constant.'
date_and_recency: Execration Ritual: Version 1, April 2008 (eScholarship 2008-04-03); no later version seen. Violence: Version 1, November 2015. Material discussed spans from at least the early Old Kingdom to the Roman Period; Mirgissa deposit is Middle Kingdom; Avaris human victim early 18th Dynasty; daily and festival execrations 'at least by the Late Period'; Gee's Karnak priesthood Ptolemaic. Both are reference syntheses and do not reflect finds or scholarship after their dates.
key_claims: 1) Definition: execration was a stylized magical rite to prevent rebellion by Egyptians, foreigners or supernatural forces by destroying enemies 'textually and kinetically' through inanimate, animal or human substitutes. 2) Duration: from at least the early Old Kingdom through the Roman Period; attested throughout Pharaonic history. 3) Origins: bound-prisoner iconography and the smashing of red offering pots (after Assmann 1994), with ties to purification rites; by the Old Kingdom pot-smashing had produced independent execration rites. 4) Texts: from simple lists of names to substantial formulae; standardized by the Middle Kingdom; key manuscripts are P. Bremner-Rhind (Theban version), P. Louvre 3129 and P. BM 10252 (Abydos version, Urk. VI), and P. Salt 825. 5) Targets: political, preternatural and personal enemies, often tied together; the Book of Felling Apophis says the rite fells the enemies of Ra, Horus and Pharaoh. Victims are named for what they 'would in the future' do (future relative sDmtj.fj), so the rite is proactive and apotropaic. 6) State and private use: standardization and geographic knowledge point to state sponsorship; uninscribed or name-only figures at private graves show individual use. 7) Materials: red pots first; by the late Old Kingdom also papyrus, hairballs, figurines, statues and statuettes of clay, stone, wax or wood; likely live animals. Wax figures and a fresh sheet of papyrus with the name were among the commonest materials, judging by Bremner-Rhind. 8) Archaeological bias: perishable victims are mostly invisible, so surviving (mostly clay) remains are 'a vast under-representation of the frequency of the rite'. 9) Mirgissa is the most complete find, including melted wax, pots, mud and limestone figures and one decapitated human. 10) Actions: binding, smashing, stomping, stabbing, cutting, spearing, spitting, locking in a box, burning, soaking in urine, and almost always burial. 11) Purpose: 'to prevent chaotic forces from acting before they could even begin.' 12) Violence (2015): execration figures were smashed, decapitated, mutilated, stabbed, speared, burned and buried; violence against mortals and preternatural enemies was combined; the Apophis-Sun God conflict is an 'ongoing battle' personifying chaos versus order; destroying chaotic enemies restores order; ritual slaying stayed constant over time.
headline_figures: - 'Over 1,000 execration deposits have been found' (count of deposits, mostly in cemeteries; 10 named sites). - Mirgissa (Middle Kingdom fortress): 'nearly 200 broken inscribed red vases', 'over 400 broken uninscribed red vases', 'nearly 350 mud figurines', 'four limestone figures', 'one human' (head 'ritually severed and buried upside down'); basis: Ritner 1993: 153-154 and Vila 1973; figures are rounded ('nearly', 'over'). - Quoted rite (Schott 1929: 5): 'spit on him four times'. - Faulkner page references for daily and cyclical festival execrations: Faulkner 1937: 169, 171, 174. - Violence (2015): 'At least two execration rituals' used humans (Mirgissa, Avaris).
dating_and_context: Dating is by archaeological context and textual tradition as summarized from secondary literature. Deposits come mostly from cemeteries (Semna, Uronarti, Mirgissa, Elephantine, Thebes, Balat, Abydos, Helwan, Saqqara, Giza). Mirgissa is a Middle Kingdom Nubian fortress deposit (Vila 1963, 1973). Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a) evidence is early 18th Dynasty (Fuscaldo 2003). Ritual manuscripts: Abydos version from the temple of Osiris (P. Louvre 3129, P. BM 10252); Theban version from the temple of Amonrasonter (P. Bremner-Rhind = P. BM 10188); P. Salt 825 = P. BM 10051. Ptolemaic performance space identified in the temple of Montu at Karnak (Gee, forthcoming at the time). Muhlestein does not give a specific date for P. Bremner-Rhind.
what_it_says_about_apophis: The 2008 entry names 'The Book of Felling Apophis' (Faulkner's Bremner-Rhind sections) as the example of political and preternatural enemies being tied together: the rite fells the enemies of Ra, Horus and Pharaoh. It treats Bremner-Rhind as the Theban version of the execration ritual and as the best indication of materials (wax figures, fresh papyrus with the name). It cites Faulkner for the idea that those who know creation can eliminate their own enemies, linking execration with re-creation. It says that at least by the Late Period there were daily and cyclical festival execrations, citing Faulkner 1937 (the Apophis book). The 2015 Violence entry calls it 'the ongoing battle between Apophis and the Sun God', a personification of chaos against order, and says destroying such enemies 'represents a restoration of order'. Neither entry claims Apophis is ever finally defeated; neither entry describes the sun's night journey in detail.
ritual_practice: Objects: red pots (earliest, smashed probably with a pestle), papyrus, hairballs, figurines, statues and statuettes of clay, stone, wax or wood, likely live animals, and in at least two cases humans (Mirgissa, Avaris). Wax figures and a fresh papyrus sheet bearing the target's name were among the commonest materials per Bremner-Rhind. Actions: bound, smashed, stomped on, stabbed, cut, speared, spat on, locked in a box, burned, soaked in urine, then almost always buried, sometimes upside down. A quoted rite (Schott 1929: 5): spit four times, trample with the left foot, smite with a spear, slaughter with a knife, place on the fire, spit on him in the fire many times. Each action could need its own rite and a full rite could repeat actions 'numerous times with numerous figures'. Who: state-sponsored performances (standardized texts, foreign geography) and small private rites by individuals; in the Ptolemaic period a specific priestly line performed them for generations in the temple of Montu at Karnak (after Gee). Where: deposits mostly in cemeteries; temple versions at Abydos and Thebes.
prescribed_vs_attested_frequency: Prescribed: 'at least by the Late Period there were also both daily and cyclical festival execrations (Faulkner 1937: 169, 171, 174)'; other rites 'arose due to specific circumstances'. Attested: over 1,000 deposits, but Muhlestein states that perishable victims (animals, hair, papyrus, wood, wax) are 'largely archaeologically invisible', so the mostly clay remains are 'a vast under-representation of the frequency of the rite'. Private, small-scale rituals are 'far less archaeologically visible'. He gives no count of performances; the gap between daily prescription and surviving evidence is explained by material survival rather than shown to be a gap in practice.
relevance_to_angle: Strongly supports the maintenance reading. The rite is proactive and preventive: victims are named for what they 'would in the future' do, and the stated purpose is 'to prevent chaotic forces from acting before they could even begin'. Daily and festival execrations (Late Period) make it a recurring routine, not a one-off triumph. The Violence entry frames the Apophis conflict as an 'ongoing battle' and says ritual slaying 'appears to have remained constant'. It also notes ongoing kinetic violence built into objects (door pivots, chariot wheels, bows) that re-enact defeat with every use. Complication: the rite also served immediate political ends against specific enemies and could involve real human victims, so it is not purely a cosmic housekeeping chore; and much of its frequency is inferred, not counted.
limitations_stated: Execration Ritual: perishable materials are 'largely archaeologically invisible, making the known (mostly clay) remains of the ritual a vast under-representation of the frequency of the rite'; 'Private, small-scale rituals are far less archaeologically visible'; 'not every execration included all of the following components'. Hedged wording: Assmann 'suggests' the pot origin; standardization is 'perhaps indicating' a standard form; live animals 'likely' used; 'If the Bremner-Rhind Papyrus is any indication'. Violence (2015): 'Our knowledge of violence in ancient Egypt is largely determined by the nature of the sources available' and 'We must use caution when retrojecting later views about violence to earlier periods, though often, all we have is later evidence.'
source_discrepancies: [uncertain] Muhlestein's Mirgissa figures are rounded ('nearly 200', 'over 400', 'nearly 350'); exact counts in Vila or Ritner were not checked here. Muhlestein (2008) states the Mirgissa human was a victim as fact, while his 2015 entry hedges ('almost certainly used humans'). He gives Faulkner 1938 as JEA 24(1) pp. 41-53, matching one of the page ranges noted in the sibling Bremner-Rhind result (which also reports 41-52 in some bibliographies). He places Bremner-Rhind in the temple of Amonrasonter at Thebes; its date (c. 305 BC per the Attalus header noted in the Bremner-Rhind result) is not given in the UEE entry. The 2008 PDF's internal 'Full Citation' URL (digital2.library.ucla.edu ark) differs from the eScholarship permalink; same work.
verification_status: All quotes and claims attributed to Muhlestein checked against the full PDFs of both UEE entries actually opened (via Wayback copies of the eScholarship PDFs). Claims Muhlestein makes about underlying sources (Mirgissa counts from Vila 1973 and Ritner 1993; Schott 1929: 5 rite wording; Faulkner 1937 on daily and festival execrations; Fuscaldo 2003 on Avaris; Gee on the Montu temple priesthood) were NOT checked against those primary sources: [uncertain] as to the underlying sources, verified only as Muhlestein's statements.
